doc.title: Clay Jenkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 18, 2016

chapter: Snooky Young and the Basie feel
title: Snooky from Lunceford to Basie and the upbeat accent
summary: Snooky had to relearn playing going from Lunceford to Basie, and Jenkins credits Basie's upbeat accents with influencing bop.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: I have this wonderful moment with him talking with Gerald Wilson and they were talking about going from the Lunceford band —
Right, they left the same day.
And went to the Basie band, and Snooky said, “I had to learn how to play all over.”

That’s right he told me that too. Because he said Lunceford’s band was like a show band kind of two-beat band. And Basie was in four swinging. And he said a few times, he said, “I’m not making this.” And the guys in Basie’s band said, “yes, Snooky, you’re doing okay.” Marshall Royal said, “yeah, you’re doing okay.” And Snooky said, “I’m not making it.” He said, “yeah, yeah, yeah, you are.” He told me that several times. And he’s the voice of that band. And I tell my students the thing with Snooky is the accent with

him is what got the dynamic of the band. The accents where he put the accents, that was the dynamic of the band, and everything else was softer. So the accents made it dance and swing and bounce. And to me, and I think I’m right about this, I’m not very dogmatic about very many things, but he was on the band with Lester Young. And early on he knew Lester Young, he knew Billie Holliday, he knew all those people. And the band went through Kansas City well who was listening to Lester Young? Charlie Parker. And so to me Lester Young’s style and the Basie style is what influenced the bop style. Accents on the upbeat. And that thing that just made it dance. Where the swing band beforehand that the accents had been on the downbeat. Like Benny Goodman and even players like Coleman Hawkins and Ben — it was on the downbeat. But Basie’s band it was like dancing. And I just think that was so incredibly important. So I give a lot of credit to Snooky.
Boy that stuff, how do you point to one person, from what you’re describing, that feel, that offbeat thing.

Well I think really it’s the rhythm section and they were kind of — the way that Basie played. Because he was really a great player. He was really like [scats]. I don’t know if boogaloo is the right word, but just a jump.

Yeah, yeah. Like a jump band. I really think it came from the rhythm section [scats] that kind of stuff. So the upbeat [scats]. Which is much more modern swing. That’s the way we still play. And people, if they have trouble with that, they have trouble with it. It’s the weirdest thing. And being around Snooky — one time my wife said, “you can never leave the Clayton band because you play the way you play because you sat next to Snooky Young all those years.” And it’s true. And I mean we solo totally different. When Snooky soloed he was more downbeat. But when he played lead oh my gracious. There was nothing like playing in a section with Snooky Young playing lead. There was nothing like it. So he’s definitely the father of that. And really I think if you asked anybody, Jon Faddis or any trumpet player, or Byron Stripling or anybody like that, they’d say no, Snooky Young. Yeah definitely.
